name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
family: Vertical pull (own parent; shoulder extension, arms straight)

claims.text: The cable is set at the highest pulley position and a straight bar is held overhand, hands about shoulder width or a little wider.

quotes.text: Start by setting the cable machine to the highest pulley position.
Take hold of the bar with an overhand grip, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Stand facing a cable stack machine and hold a straight handle overhead with a grip outside shoulder width.

claims.text: Stand facing the stack, a step back so the cable is already under tension, feet about hip to shoulder width, knees soft.

quotes.text: Step back just enough so the cable has tension before you even start the movement. Plant your feet shoulder-width apart, soften your knees, and hinge slightly forward at the hips.
Stand with the feet hip-width apart, the hips straight, the back tall, and the knees slightly bent.

claims.text: Sources disagree on the hips: one coach source asks for a slight forward hip hinge so the lats start stretched, while ACE describes the hips straight. Both keep the back tall and the trunk still.

quotes.text: If you stand perfectly vertical, you cut the range of motion short and lose the stretch at the top.
Stand with the feet hip-width apart, the hips straight, the back tall, and the knees slightly bent.

claims.text: The arms stay nearly straight, with only a slight elbow bend, from top to bottom.

quotes.text: Keep your chest up and shoulders pulled back. Your elbows should have a slight bend, but the arms stay nearly straight throughout.
Keeping the trunk braced and the arms straight, bring the bar down into contact with the front of the body, then return to the top under control.
Keep the arms straight while bringing the hands down to the front of the waist.

claims.text: The bar travels down in an arc and stops when the hands reach the front of the thighs or body, chest still tall and trunk braced.

quotes.text: Stop when your hands reach the front of your thighs, keeping your chest tall and core braced.
Keeping the trunk braced and the arms straight, bring the bar down into contact with the front of the body, then return to the top under control.

claims.text: Bending the elbows is named the most common fault: it turns the lift into a bent-arm pulldown or a triceps pushdown instead of a lat exercise.

quotes.text: This is the most common way lifters ruin the Straight Arm Pulldown.
Once you bend the elbows, you’re no longer pulling with the lats, you’re turning it into a Bent Arm Pulldown or a Triceps Pushdown.

claims.text: The weight should be light enough to move smoothly and hold a one-second squeeze at the bottom; going too heavy brings jerking, torso swing and momentum.

quotes.text: Going too heavy leads to jerking the bar, swinging your torso, and relying on momentum instead of muscle.
Drop the ego, lighten the load, and move the bar smoothly from top to bottom. If you can’t pause at the bottom for a one-second squeeze, the weight is too heavy.

claims.text: The way back up is slow and controlled, letting the lats lengthen at the top instead of letting the stack pull the arms up.

quotes.text: Don’t let the stack yank your arms back up. Instead, guide the weight slowly, letting your lats lengthen and stretch under control at the top.
Slowly lift the hands back to the starting position to lower the weight.

claims.text: The spine stays neutral: over-arching the lower back moves stress onto the lumbar spine, and feeling it in the lower back more than the lats means the setup is off.

quotes.text: Rounding the upper back shortens the lats and reduces their involvement, while over-arching the lower back shifts stress onto the lumbar spine instead of the lats.
If you feel this exercise in your lower back more than your lats, your setup is off. Brace like you’re about to take a punch in the stomach then move only your arms.

claims.text: The pulling cable tries to draw the torso forward, so the abdominal muscles brace to stop the lower back arching.

quotes.text: The cable is trying to yank your torso forward, and without proper bracing, you’ll arch your lower back and shift tension away from the lats.

claims.text: The lats are the main target; the exercise trains them with little biceps, delt and upper-back work compared with rows and bent-arm pulldowns.

quotes.text: The straight-arm pulldown strengthens the lats without involving the biceps, delts and upper back like most row, pulldown and other upper body pulling exercises.
The latissimus dorsi are the prime movers here.

claims.text: The long head of the triceps crosses the shoulder and helps extend it, so the back of the upper arm assists; the rear delts assist only slightly.

quotes.text: Because it crosses the shoulder joint, it also helps with shoulder extension and this is the same action the lats perform.
They also assist slightly in shoulder extension, though their contribution is small compared to the lats.

claims.text: EMG comparisons with the barbell pullover (20 adults) found the pullover did not raise lat or triceps activity over the straight-arm pulldown, and a review said the pulldown may offer a more targeted back stimulus, depending on grip configuration. Measured, but one small study reported through a review.

quotes.text: When comparing the barbell pullover with the straight-arm pulldown across different grip widths in a sample of 20 healthy, physically active adults, the pullover generally produced higher overall EMG amplitude for most muscles studied, with the notable exception of the latissimus dorsi and triceps brachii
The straight-arm pulldown, by contrast, may offer a more targeted stimulus to the dorsal musculature depending on grip configuration.

claims.text: For intermediate to advanced lifters with an eventual emphasis on heavy loads (1-6 RM), ACSM advises a moderate speed of 1-2 seconds up and 1-2 seconds down; the plate uses it only as a drawing convention for tempo. Load goes up by 2-10% once the target reps are beaten by one or two.

quotes.text: with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

sources.title: How To Do The Straight Arm Pulldown
Electromyographic Analysis of Latissimus Dorsi Activation During Common Resistance Training Exercises: A Narrative Review
American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults

plate.viewWhy: The movement is shoulder extension in one plane (c4, c5, c12): the arm arc and the elbow angle, which carries the main fault (c6), both read from the side.
plate.equipment: Cable column with the pulley at its highest point and a straight bar (c1). The lifter stands a step back from the stack so the cable is taut at the top (c2).
plate.start: Standing, feet hip to shoulder width, knees soft (c2); trunk tall with at most a slight forward hip lean (c3); arms up toward the high pulley, bar held overhead, elbows almost straight with a slight bend (c1, c4); cable taut (c2).
plate.end: Same trunk angle as the start (c3, c7); arms swept down in an arc, elbows still almost straight (c4); bar at the front of the thighs (c5); chest tall (c5).

checkpoints.label: Arms stay straight
checkpoints.what: The elbow keeps the same slight bend from top to bottom; only the shoulder moves.

checkpoints.label: Trunk still
checkpoints.what: The trunk keeps one angle all set: no swing to start the rep and no arching of the lower back.

checkpoints.label: Bar to thighs
checkpoints.what: The bar finishes at the front of the thighs, chest tall.

mistake.what: Elbows bend as the bar comes down, turning it into a bent-arm pulldown or pushdown.
mistake.why: Named the most common fault; the triceps and arms take over from the lats.

tells.text: Elbow angle the same top to bottom

grip.type: Overhand on a straight bar (c1). Rope and neutral-grip versions exist but are not drawn.
grip.width: About shoulder width or a little wider (c1).
grip.thumb: Wrapped: the hold archetype default (GA 3.1). No exercise-specific source compares thumb positions here.
grip.handContact: Hold archetype default (GA 3.1): bar across the middle of the palm, fingers wrapped. No exercise-specific source.
grip.wrist: Hold archetype default (GA 3.1): neutral, in line with the forearm. No exercise-specific source.

setup.step: Set the pulley at its highest point and attach a straight bar.
Take the bar overhand, hands about shoulder width or a little wider.
Step back until the cable is taut with your arms up; feet hip to shoulder width, knees soft.
Chest up, trunk braced, at most a slight lean forward from the hips.
Pick a weight you can move smoothly with a one-second squeeze at the bottom.

posture.point: Elbows keep a slight bend that does not change during the rep.
The bar sweeps down in an arc to the front of the thighs.
Trunk braced and still; no swing, no lower-back arch.
Slow way back up, letting the arms rise under control.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows to push the bar down.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep the same slight elbow bend all set.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Too much weight, so the torso swings and the bar is jerked down.
handlingMistakes.fix: Lower the weight until you can move smoothly and pause for a second at the bottom.
Brace the stomach and move only the arms.

rows.means: The faults the coach source warns about here are arching the lower back and swinging the torso.
rows.fix: Brace and move only the arms.

rows.means: The fault the coach source warns about here is bending the elbows, which turns it into a pushdown.
rows.fix: Keep the same slight elbow bend top to bottom.

rows.means: The coach source says going too heavy brings jerking, torso swing and momentum.
rows.fix: Drop the weight until you can pause at the bottom.

risks.risk: Arching the lower back under the pull of the cable moves stress onto the lumbar spine.
Jerking a load that is too heavy swings the torso and relies on momentum.

zooms.right: Arm almost straight, same slight bend at the top and at the bottom.
zooms.wrong: Elbow bent to about a right angle at the bottom, like a pushdown.

zooms.right: Trunk braced and still, chest tall at the bottom.

libraryDiff.why: exercises.json lists lats primary and triceps secondary, which c11, c12 and c13 support. rear_delts is added to the feel spec as secondary on coach-source mechanics only (c12), too thin to change the library entry.

notes: ACE page 334 is short and mixes a straight bar and 'one end of the rope'; only its stance, arm and tempo lines are used. The Muyor 2022 pullover vs straight-arm pulldown paper (Appl Sci 12:11138) could not be opened (MDPI 403), so it is cited only through the Di Fonza 2026 review. No source was found for a tier-specific way out or for thumb position; the hand lines are the GA hold archetype defaults. Teixeira 2022 (isometric shoulder angles) was dropped: its abstract does not support a range-of-motion cue and no line used it.
